builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Precedent or Intent? What Coding Agents Follow When Evolving Existing Code
summary: This replaces implicit reliance on repository examples and agent defaults with explicit written priority rules for handling conflicts between existing code and new instructions. Costs are limited to curating local precedent files and loading short priority rules into the agent harness, with negligible compute overhead. Failure occurs when rules are ambiguous, contradict strong local precedent, or omit the rationale needed for agents to resolve conflicting instructions.
rationale: It directly improves coding-agent reliability in production using only prompt and harness changes, requiring no additional infrastructure.
technique: Repository precedence rules for coding agents

claims.statement: This replaces implicit reliance on repository examples and agent defaults with explicit written priority rules for handling conflicts between existing code and new instructions. Costs are limited to curating local precedent files and loading short priority rules into the agent harness, with negligible compute overhead. Failure occurs when rules are ambiguous, contradict strong local precedent, or omit the rationale needed for agents to resolve conflicting instructions.
Written priority rules achieve 59/60 joint successes versus 38/60 for code examples alone, and a harness-loaded rule raises joint success from 0/120 to 117/120 in open-source repositories.
